text.p: Nearly 17,000 people had $4.8 million restored to their 401(k) retirement plans after employers made use of a grace period to replace funds they had failed to deposit properly, the government said Friday.

The Labour Department released data showing that 170 small to mid-sized businesses voluntarily returned employee contributions and made good on lost earnings after they were given six months to do so without penalty.

The amnesty programme, which expired earlier this month, was part of a broader Clinton administration effort to end fraudulent activity in 401(k) plans. So far, the crackdown has resulted in investigations that have led to the return of another $10 million in employee funds.

"We don't have any evidence the problem is widespread but ... there are going to be a few rotten apples," Labour Secretary Robert Reich said in an interview. "We at the Labour Department have to continue to act aggressively."
As a result of the grace period, contributions were repaid to plans affecting 16,800 participants. Amounts ranged from $43 to more than $200,000, the department said.

The employers, which included technology companies, law firms, physicians and credit unions among others, admitted to being delinquent for reasons ranging from computer errors to diverting funds to pay bills.
Amnesty was not an option for those employers "who had engaged in the most egregious conduct," the department said.

Companies were disqualified, for example, if they were already the subject of a criminal investigation or if they failed to make deposits that exceeded the total amount of employee contributions for all of 1995.
Some 23.4 million people participated in more than 170,000 401(k) plans with total combined assets of $613 billion in 1993, the latest year for which data are available.

The retirement plan is named for the part of the U.S. tax code that allows workers to deduct a portion of income before it is taxed, invest it and pay no taxes on the money until it is withdrawn at retirement.
Reich cautioned employees to check their 401(k) statements against their paystubs on a regular basis to ensure that their contributions have been posted accurately.
"There is no substitute for diligence on the part of employees," Reich said.
The department launched its 401(k) enforcement programme in 1995 after it received an increased number of complaints about the plans.
It issued a new rule last month that requires employers to deposit money withheld from workers' checks for 401(k) plans within 15 days instead of 90 days.
